messages.subject: [statnet_help] Measuring asymmetries
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a directed communication network among men and women. I already
tested whether ties are significantly more probable among same-sex nodes
with

mod1 <- ergm(net_simp~edges+nodematch("gender"))

giving

edges            -10.290038   0.008076      0  <1e-04 ***
nodematch.gender   0.441783   0.008740      0  <1e-04 ***

for which I derive that same-sex communication is 55% more likely.


Now how can I test whether there's any asymmetry in
the communication patterns? That is, whether men send
out significantly less (more) messages to women than women to men. Is it
possible?

Thanks

Best
Francesco Bailo

Dear all,

I would like to ask a follow-up question to a discussion that has popped up
in this forum several times before regarding the use of a single ERG model
to describe multiple networks. In my situation I have multiple
cross-sectional observations of a network through time, but I am not
interested in formation/dissolution of ties (as in the tergm case).
Instead, I would like to use information from all the networks to build a
single ergm while acknowledging that ties cannot be formed between nodes
across networks. Many of the nodes are the same across networks, but not
all of them, so the total number of nodes in each network fluctuates
slightly. My network is also directed.

I understand that this problem can perhaps be addressed using "structural
zeros" to prohibit ties across networks. I am also aware that this issue
has been discussed in some detail already in this previous post (
http://mailman13.u.washington.edu/pipermail/statnet_help/2012/001214.html).

My question is specifically about the implementation discussed in the
previous post -- I am not certain that I fully understand the given
description and would like to make sure that I get it right. Below is some
simulated data and example code that I am hoping someone here might be able
to confirm whether it implements the previous solution properly:

#simulate networks
> net1 <- network(10, directed=T, density=.2)
> net2 <- network(8, directed=T, density=.2)

#create a joint adjacency matrix
> combined <- as.network(bdiag(as.matrix.network(net1),
as.matrix.network(net2)), directed=T, matrix.type="adjacency") #create a
joint adjacency matrix and

# set attributes: unique group for each network and names that reflect some
of the same nodes in each graph

> set.vertex.attribute(combined, "vertex.names", c(1:10, 1:8))
> set.vertex.attribute(combined, "group",
c(rep("A",length(network.vertex.names(net1))), rep("B",
length(network.vertex.names(net2)))))


> (m1 <- ergm(combined ~ edges + nodemix("group")))  # should there be a
"base=" argument within nodemix?

Observed statistic(s) mix.group.B.A and mix.group.A.B are at their smallest
attainable values. Their coefficients will be fixed at -Inf.

MLE Coefficients:
        edges  mix.group.A.A  mix.group.B.A  mix.group.A.B  mix.group.B.B
      -1.1963         0.1271           -Inf           -Inf             NA

#alternatively should I set categories 1 and 4 (categories within networks)
to base to get rid of them?

> summary(combined~nodemix("group"))

mix.group.A.A mix.group.B.A mix.group.A.B mix.group.B.B
           23             0             0            13

> (m2<- ergm(combined ~ edges + nodemix("group", base=c(1,4))))

Observed statistic(s) mix.group.B.A and mix.group.A.B are at their smallest
attainable values. Their coefficients will be fixed at -Inf.

MLE Coefficients:
        edges  mix.group.B.A  mix.group.A.B
       -1.117           -Inf           -Inf

###

In particular, if someone could help me understand whether "m1" or "m2"
above achieves the described goal I would be very grateful. Finally, if one
of the above approaches is appropriate, I am also curious if it is possible
to model the non-independence of the same nodes occurring in multiple
networks (similar to a random intercept term in a GLMM for nodeID in this
case). It seems like "hergm" might be used for this purpose but I am having
trouble finding resources.

Thank you very much in advance for the help and your continued work on
these resources,

Tom

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

What you are describing is essentially the same data structure as in a 
TERGM (*not* STERGM) without temporal dependencies, a.k.a. pooled ERGM. 
See here for details: 
http://people.reed.edu/~ahm//polnet2015/TERGM%20Workshop%20Leifeld%202015-06-17/btergm-paper.pdf

This can be conveniently estimated using the xergm package, more 
specifically the btergm function (for pseudolikelihood estimation with 
bias correction via bootstrapping) and the mtergm function (for MCMC 
MLE). Both have the same syntax and model terms as the ergm function 
because ergm's model specification is used internally (i.e., you can 
integrate it in your statnet workflow). Multiple networks are handed 
over to the formula by wrapping them in a list. No need to use 
structural zeros with this approach.

Your example can be respecified as follows:

library("statnet")
net1 <- network(10, directed=T, density=.2)
net2 <- network(8, directed=T, density=.2)
library("xergm")
l <- list(net1, net2)
m1 <- btergm(l ~ edges + mutual)  # or m1 <- mtergm(l ~ edges + mutual)

If you need to control for differential tie probability of nodes across 
networks, this is essentially a dependency across networks that can be 
implemented via edgecov terms (like a fixed effect). Temporal 
dependencies are described in the paper referenced above. E.g., you can 
provide a list of matrices where 1 indicates a specific actor (in all 
matrices in the list). Note that this requires as many edgecov terms as 
there are unique nodes, but perhaps you don't need this for all actors. 
Random effects such as the ones you are describing are currently not 
implemented. I have never used hergm before, so I cannot comment on its 
ability to do this.

Best,
Philip

I think what you are looking for is nodemix.? Below is from the ergm-terms help file:
   
   - nodemix(attrname, base=NULL) (binary), nodemix(attrname, base=NULL, form="sum") (valued)
      - Nodal attribute mixing: The attrname argument is a character vector giving the names of categorical attributes in the network's vertex attribute list. By default, this term adds one network statistic to  the model for each possible pairing of attribute values. The statistic equals the number of edges in the network in which the nodes have that pairing of values. (When multiple names are given, a statistic is added for each combination of attribute values for those names.) In other words, this term produces one statistic for every entry in the mixing matrix for the attribute(s). The ordering of the attribute values is alphabetical (for nominal categories) or numerical (for ordered categories). The optional base argument is a vector of integers corresponding to the pairings that should not be included. If base contains only negative integers, then these integers correspond to the only pairings that should be included. By default (i.e., with base=NULL or base=0), all pairings are included.
   -    

Also, given that you see "fails" as a factor, you likely don't want to use nodecov as it is for numeric variables.

Hi all,

My coauthor and I are interested in assessing how individuals belonging to
different groups vary in their tendency to form network ties following a
triadic closure logic. In other words, we are interested in answering the
following question: are individuals belonging to one group more likely to
close triads than individuals belonging to the other group? Here is a
simple example: assume we have three age groups and we have reason to
believe that individuals in the youngest age group are more likely to close
triads than those in the two other age groups.

Two questions:

1. Any references to papers implementing such a hypothesis test using an
ERGM?
2. Any suggestions on how to implement a test of this hypothesis in
Statnet's ergm function? Intuitively, one would include an interaction
effect of the nodefactor variable and the network statistic.

Thanks for your help!

messages.body_plain:
Srecko, the syntax for nodemix is:

nodemix(attrname, base)

So, in your case it sounds like this should be

nodemix("fail_count_factor")

To get the default model, which omits the last category for the reference 
group.

In order to create a special reference category, I'd suggest you do a bit 
of exploratory work first:

mixingmatrix("fail_count_factor")

To look at the mixing pattern that nodemix will be representing

And then to see how nodemix works:

summary(gnsocial ~ nodemix("fail_count_factor"))
summary(gnsocial ~ nodemix("fail_count_factor", base=1))
summary(gnsocial ~ nodemix("fail_count_factor", base=c(0,1))

etc.

Note that once you put an edges term in, you've used a degree of freedom, 
so you'll have one less for the nodemix term

summary(gnsocial ~ edges + nodemix("fail_count_factor"))

Basically, learn to use the terms, and make sure you understand what they 
do.

hth,
Martina

(i.e., element-wise product) of the covariate matrix and the matrix 
containing the change statistic and include that as an interaction term 
in your model. However, you may need to compute the change statistic 
manually or dig really deep into the code of the ergm package to compute 
the change statistic directly.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Francesco,

Note that xergm is not part of statnet. We should probably continue to 
discuss this bilaterally as I don't want to hijack the statnet-help list 
for xergm-related questions.

btergm corrects the uncertainty measures of the MPLE estimates by means 
of bootstrapping because the standard errors are otherwise inherently 
biased. So it's probably a bad idea to compute anything related to 
uncertainty from mod_xergm@effects. The bootstrapping results are saved 
in mod_xergm@bootsamp, but I don't know if that's helpful: E.g., I wrote 
a btergm.se function a while ago, which computes standard errors from 
that, but they are only valid if the samples are normally distributed, 
which is not always the case (the btergm.se function therefore generally 
prints a warning message). That said, you can also use the mtergm 
function to compute estimates and uncertainty measures for TERGMs via 
MCMC MLE. It is just going to be prohibitively slow for anything larger 
than a few networks, which is why I wrote btergm in the first place. 
mtergm returns an ergm object, and I believe there is a vcov method 
available for ergm objects.

Best,
Philip

> model fit with btergm of the xergm package. I tried to write few lines
> of code to compute it (based on the formula for the logistic
> regression). Can anyone confirm that the code is correct? Is there any
> substantial reason for not implementing vcov() for btergmobjects?
>
> require(xergm)
>
> mod_xergm <- mod_xergm(...)
>
> X <- as.matrix(mod_xergm@effects)
> beta.hat <- as.matrix(coef(mod_xergm))
>
> require(slam)
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM Dyadic Covariate Issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

My name is Maureen McCusker, and I?m a graduate student at Virginia Tech, earning my Ph.D. in I/O Psychology. First of all, thank you for making yourselves available. I am writing to you because I have been working on on a project running an ERGM model for several months and have been struggling with my dyadic covariate term. To give you a little background, I am analyzing some data on dyadic leadership perceptions within 11 teams of 9, where the outcome is a dichotomous rating. In addition to several other predictors in the model (icov, ocov, absdiff), my model includes 2 edcov terms: the structural zero matrix, reflecting the teams, and the directed dyadic covariate. I have seen the dyadic covariate matrix read into R using run using two different codes, and I am receiving error codes for both (please see below).  I am wondering if you might be able to tell me which is the correct R code for dyadic covariates, and for the correct one, what the error code means.

For the following code, Beh is the dyadic covariate term.  

1. The first code I?m using simply reads the data in as a CSV, converts it to a matrix, and then converts it to a network. In the ERGM code itself, I run the network in as an edcov term (see this below). When I run this method, the dyadic covariate term is HIGHLY unstable and changes values as signs with a slight change in the parameters, such MCMC sample size. I also receive a message stating that I likely have highly correlated terms, which is what I assume is driving the instability in the dyadic covariate term. When I check MCMC Diagnostics, I find that the dyadic covariate and the edges term are perfectly correlated at 1.0. I know there have been some recent findings that ERGM may have some issues with small groups and also that there are potentially some problems with highly correlated model terms. If this is the correct way to run the dyadic covariate term, do you have any ideas of how I can fix this issue?  R Code: 
#reading behavior file

Beh <- read.csv("Behaviors_Matrix.csv", header = FALSE)

Beh.mat1<-as.matrix(Beh)

Beh.mat2<-apply(Beh.mat1,1,as.numeric)

Beh.mat2[is.na(Beh.mat2)]<-0

Beh.mat2

Beh.net <-as.network.matrix(Beh.mat2,directed=T,matrix.type="adjacency?)

And then here is the ERGM: 

New_Model_2_beh_2<-ergm(DV.net ~edges+ostar(2)+ mutual + twopath + istar(2) + edgecov(Struc_Zero.net) + edgecov(tasks.net)+ nodeocov("Dom")+nodeocov("Self_Eff")+nodeicov("SAT_Tot") +nodeicov("Dom") +nodeicov("Self_Eff") +nodeicov("Self_Mon") + absdiff("Self_Mon")+absdiff("Dom") + dyadcov(Beh.net), eval.loglik=TRUE,  seed=20, burnin=2000, interval=50, MCMCsamplesize=100000, maxit=10, control=control.ergm(steplength=.25))

summary(New_Model_2_beh_2)

2. The second way I?m running the model is similar to the way that another researcher, who I know also posted on Statnet_help regarding a similar issue back in February, ran hers. When I do it this way, I receive the same error message she received (In m[tl[!nal] + (hl[!nal] - 1) * network.size(x)] <- val[!nal] : number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length). Using this strategy, I first create a megamatrix of all possible ties, then I run in a matrix of all the dyadic ?attributes? to assign to the ties, then I assign attributes to the ?all-possible ties" matrix. The edgecov term in the ERGM is also different. Please see below: 

#reading behavior file
Beh <- read.csv("Behaviors_Matrix.csv", header = FALSE)
Beh.mat1<-as.matrix(Beh)
Beh.mat2<-apply(Beh.mat1,1,as.numeric)
Beh.mat2[is.na(Beh.mat2)]<-0 
Beh.mat2
Beh.net <-as.network.matrix(Beh.mat2,directed=T,matrix.type="adjacency")
summary(Beh.net)

#making all possible ties matrix: 
Poss_ties<- read.csv("poss_ties_mat2.csv", header = FALSE) 
Poss_ties.mat1<-as.matrix(Poss_ties)
Poss_ties.mat2<-apply(Poss_ties.mat1, 1, as.numeric)
Poss_ties.net<-as.network.matrix(Poss_ties,directed=F,matrix.type="adjacency?)

#assigning behaviors to possible ties 
set.edge.attribute(Poss_ties.net,"Beh.net",Beh.net)

The ERGM for strategy 2 is then as follows: 
New_Model_2<-ergm(DV.net ~edges+ostar(2)+ mutual + twopath + istar(2) + edgecov(tasks.net) + edgecov(Poss_ties.net,attrname="Beh.net")+ edgecov(Struc_Zero.net) + nodeocov("Dom")+nodeocov("Self_Eff")+nodeicov("SAT_Tot") +nodeicov("Dom") +nodeicov("Self_Eff") +nodeicov("Self_Mon") + absdiff("Self_Mon")+absdiff("Dom"), eval.loglik=TRUE,  seed=20, burnin=3000, interval=50, MCMCsamplesize=50000, maxit=10, control=control.ergm(steplength=.25))

As you can see, for both of these strategies, I employ a structural zero matrix. The structural zero matrix has given me problems since i started because the output because the output produces a ?-INF? estimate and NA for standard errors. Perhaps this is part of the issue. 


Thank you in advance for your help.

Maureen
